objectives.text: Find and point to different shapes hidden in real-world objects around the room
Identify the names of basic shapes like circles, squares, triangles, and rectangles
Compare shapes by looking at their straight sides and corners

oracle.detail: question stem contains the answer "Triangle" and no distractor: "Which one is a triangle?"
3/4 answers are "B" — answers cluster instead of spreading

problems.question: Which object looks like a circle?
problems.rationale: A clock is round and curved with no corners, making it a circle. A window usually has four straight sides like a square, and a slice of pizza has three sides like a triangle.
problems.teachingNote: Have children trace shapes in the air with their finger to connect the curved outline of a circle with the round shape of the clock.
successCriteria: Identify everyday objects that are shaped like a circle
Differentiate circular objects from squares and triangles
problems.subject: MATHEMATICS

problems.question: Which object looks like a rectangle?
problems.rationale: A door is shaped like a rectangle because it has four straight sides and four square corners. A ball is completely round, which makes it a circle or sphere. An open book has curved lines and does not make a clean rectangle shape.
problems.teachingNote: Have students use their fingers to trace the two long sides and two short sides of a classroom door. Comparing straight sides to the curved shape of a ball reinforces early geometric distinctions.
successCriteria: Identify a rectangle among familiar real-world objects.
problems.subject: MATHEMATICS

problems.question: Which one is a triangle?
problems.rationale: A triangle is a shape with three straight sides and three corners. The red shape has three points, making it a triangle. Circles are round with no corners, and squares have four straight sides.
problems.teachingNote: Encourage young learners to count the three sharp corners or points on a triangle using their fingers.
successCriteria: Identify and name a triangle from a set of basic geometric shapes.
problems.subject: MATHEMATICS

problems.statement: A square has 4 corners that look the same.
problems.rationale: A square is a special shape that always has four straight sides of the exact same length and four square corners, which are all identical. Children often confuse shapes when corners do not point the same way, but a square's corners are always uniform.
problems.teachingNote: Have students use their fingers to point and count the four corners on square blocks or paper cutouts to build tactile understanding.
successCriteria: Identify the number of corners on a square
Recognize that a square has identical corners
problems.subject: MATHEMATICS

problems.question: Which shape has more straight sides?
problems.rationale: A rectangle has 4 straight sides, while a triangle has only 3 straight sides. Since 4 is a bigger number than 3, the rectangle has more sides. A circle is round and does not have any straight sides.
problems.teachingNote: Encourage students to trace and count each straight side with their finger to connect counting with geometric attributes.
successCriteria: Count the number of straight sides on basic 2D shapes.
Compare two shapes to determine which has more sides.
problems.subject: MATHEMATICS

after.notes: Students are repeatedly prompted to identify hidden shapes within real-world objects across 5 independent items.
All 4 target shapes (circle, square, triangle, rectangle) are assessed with multiple direct oral naming and identification items.
Only 1 item (shapes-final-knowledge-check#problems[7]) directly requires comparing shapes by side count; other blocks assess counting sides or construction rather than comparative evaluation.

problems.question: Two apples and one more apple make how many?
problems.rationale: When you start with two apples and add one more, you count forward by one to reach three. Combining two groups into one group makes a larger total amount. That means two plus one gives us three apples altogether.
problems.teachingNote: Have students use counters or fingers to physically represent joining two items and one item together.
successCriteria: Count to combine two small groups of objects up to five.
Identify that adding items together results in a greater quantity.
problems.subject: MATHEMATICS

problems.question: Frog hops from two to which bigger number?
problems.rationale: The number line shows a hop starting at 2 and landing on 4. When we hop forward on the number line, we are adding to reach a bigger number. Therefore, the frog lands on the new total of 4.
problems.teachingNote: Use physical movement or finger-hopping along a number path to reinforce that addition means jumping forward to larger numbers.
successCriteria: Identify the landing number after hopping forward on a number line
Understand that moving right on a number line represents adding to get a larger total
problems.subject: MATHEMATICS

packages.topic: Decoding CVC words with short a

objectives.text: Listen to and identify the short 'a' sound in spoken words.
Connect letter sounds to written letters to decode simple CVC words.
Read a short CVC word all the way through to discover the secret word.

problems.question: Which word has the short a sound?
problems.rationale: When we say 'cat', we hear the short a sound in the middle: /c/ /a/ /t/. The word 'sun' has a short u sound, and 'pig' has a short i sound.
problems.teachingNote: Have students stretch out the middle sound of each word using continuous phoneme blending (e.g., c-aaaa-t) to clearly hear the short 'a' vowel sound.
successCriteria: Identify the medial short 'a' vowel sound in spoken CVC words
Distinguish the short 'a' sound from other short vowel sounds
problems.subject: LANGUAGE_ARTS

problems.statement: The word bat has the short a sound like apple.
problems.rationale: The word bat contains the short 'a' vowel sound, just like the word apple. When we say bat, we hear the /a/ sound in the middle, which is the same sound we make at the beginning of apple.
problems.teachingNote: Help students connect the middle sound of CVC words to familiar starting sounds like the short 'a' in apple.
successCriteria: Identify the short a sound in CVC words
Compare vowel sounds between words
problems.subject: LANGUAGE_ARTS

problems.question: Which animal has the middle short a sound?
problems.rationale: The word cat has the short a sound in the middle. When we stretch out the sounds /k/, /a/, and /t/, we hear short a in the center. The words dog and pig have different middle vowel sounds.
problems.teachingNote: Have students tap out the three phonemes on their fingers (/k/ - /a/ - /t/) to isolate and emphasize the middle short vowel sound.
successCriteria: Identify the short a sound in the middle of a spoken CVC word.
Distinguish the short a sound from other short vowel sounds.
problems.subject: LANGUAGE_ARTS

problems.question: What word do the sounds m, a, and p make?
problems.rationale: Blending the beginning sound /m/, the short a vowel sound /æ/, and the ending sound /p/ creates the word "map". The word "mop" has a short o sound instead, and "cap" starts with the /k/ sound.
problems.teachingNote: Have students practice continuous blending by stretching out the sounds /mmmaaaap/ before saying the whole word smoothly.
successCriteria: Blend individual phonemes /m/, /æ/, and /p/ to decode a CVC word with short a.
problems.subject: LANGUAGE_ARTS

problems.question: Which animal has the short a sound?
problems.rationale: Cat has the short a vowel sound in the middle, like in apple. When we say cat slowly, we hear the /k/, /a/, and /t/ sounds. Dog and pig have different middle vowel sounds.
problems.teachingNote: Encourage students to open their mouths wide and make the short a sound like they are biting an apple to help isolate the medial vowel sound in CVC words.
successCriteria: Identify the medial short a vowel sound in a CVC word
Distinguish short a from other short vowel sounds
problems.subject: LANGUAGE_ARTS

problems.question: Read the word 'van' all the way through to match.
problems.rationale: The word 'van' has the starting sound /v/, the short a sound /ă/ in the middle, and the ending sound /n/. When we blend those sounds together from left to right, they make the word 'van'! A box and a cup have completely different vowel and consonant sounds.
problems.teachingNote: Guide students to tap out each sound (/v/, /ă/, /n/) with their fingers before blending them smoothly together. Emphasize the medial short 'a' sound to help students contrast it with short 'o' in box and short 'u' in cup.
successCriteria: Decode a CVC word with the short a vowel sound
Blend individual phonemes from left to right to read a whole word
problems.subject: LANGUAGE_ARTS
